## Per-chapter highlights

### Chapter 1 — The Burnt Offering (Olah)

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, messianic-prophecy, restoration

Leviticus opens with the LORD calling Moses from the Tabernacle just completed at the close of Exodus, and gives the first of five offering- types: the burnt offering (olah, "ascending"). A male without blemish from the herd, flock, or fowl, voluntarily offered, with the offerer's hand laid on its head; the whole animal consumed on the altar as "a sweet savour unto the LORD." The chapter establishes the foundational pattern — substitutionary atonement and total devotion to God — that the rest of the sacrificial system builds on.

### Chapter 2 — The Meal Offering (Minchah)

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, restoration

The meal offering (minchah) — the chapter's bloodless grain offering of fine flour, oil, and frankincense, brought raw or baked in oven, pan, or fryingpan, always with salt, never with leaven or honey. A "memorial portion" is burned on the altar as a sweet savour; the remainder belongs to Aaron and his sons as "a thing most holy." The chapter's salt-of-the-covenant provision and the bloodless-offering category fill in what the burnt offering of Lev 1 left unspecified.

### Chapter 3 — The Peace Offering (Zevach Shelamim)

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, restoration

The peace offering (zevach shelamim) — male or female of herd, flock, or goats, without blemish; hand laid on its head, blood sprinkled, the fat and kidneys and the caul above the liver burned on the altar as "the food of the offering made by fire... a sweet savour." The chapter's signature provision: all the fat belongs to the LORD; the fat and the blood may never be eaten. The peace offering is the shared-meal sacrifice — portions for God, the priest, and the offerer's family eat together before the LORD.

### Chapter 4 — The Sin Offering (Chattat), Graduated by Office

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, judgment, messianic-prophecy, restoration

The sin offering (chattat) — graduated by office and responsibility: the anointed priest brings a bullock (his sin defiles the sanctuary); the whole congregation a bullock (corporate sin); a ruler a male goat; a common person a female goat or lamb. For sins of ignorance ("through ignorance against any of the commandments"). The priest's and congregation's offerings have their bodies burned outside the camp — the pattern Hebrews 13:11-13 reads as fulfilled in Christ "suffered without the gate."

### Chapter 5 — The Trespass Offering (Asham), Restitution Plus One-Fifth

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, judgment, restoration

Specific instances triggering the trespass offering (failure to testify when called as witness, contact with uncleanness, rash oaths); the offering's three-tier accessibility (lamb, two birds, fine flour) accommodating the poor. The asham (trespass offering) proper: a ram with restitution-plus-one-fifth for inadvertent sin against "the holy things of the LORD" — the OT's first explicit combination of sacrifice with monetary reparation, anticipating the broader restitution principle of Lev 6.

### Chapter 6 — Priest's Manual: Trespass Concluded; Perpetual Fire; Offerings' Procedure

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, restoration

The trespass-offering legislation concludes (now covering deception of neighbor: restitution-plus-one-fifth, then offering). The chapter then turns to the priests with a manual of procedure for the offerings — the burnt offering's perpetual altar fire that "shall ever be burning... it shall never go out"; the meal offering eaten by the priests as their portion; the daily perpetual meal-offering of the anointed priest; the sin offering's most-holy character.

### Chapter 7 — Priest's Manual Concluded; Peace Offering Sub-Types; Priestly Portions

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, restoration

The priest's manual concludes. The trespass offering's priestly procedure; the burnt-offering skin and meal-offering remainder as priestly portions; the peace offering's three sub-types (thanksgiving, vow, freewill) with their timing requirements; the fat-and-blood prohibition restated; the wave-breast and heave- shoulder priestly portions; and the chapter's closing summary that closes the entire offerer-and-priest manual block (Lev 1-7).

### Chapter 8 — Consecration of Aaron and His Sons (Seven Days)

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, restoration, prophetic-call

Moses carries out the consecration of Aaron and his sons that Exodus 29 had prescribed. The whole congregation gathers; Aaron is washed, robed (with breastplate and Urim and Thummim), and anointed; his sons clothed and anointed; the bullock sin offering, the burnt-offering ram, and the consecration ram each killed with the prescribed blood-applications including the right ear, right thumb, and right great toe. The seven-day stay at the tent door begins. The chapter executes what Exodus 29 commanded; obedience is total.

### Chapter 9 — The Eighth Day: Fire from the LORD Consumes the Offerings

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, restoration, prophetic-call

The eighth day after the seven-day consecration: Aaron offers his first sacrifices as installed high priest — sin offering and burnt offering for himself, then the same with peace offerings for the people. He lifts up his hand and blesses the people; Moses and Aaron enter the tent, return, and bless again — and the glory of the LORD appears. Fire comes out from before the LORD and consumes the burnt offering on the altar; the people shout and fall on their faces. The sacrificial system is divinely accepted.

### Chapter 10 — Nadab and Abihu: Strange Fire

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, judgment, prophetic-call

Aaron's two eldest sons offer "strange fire" before the LORD — fire He did not command — and are consumed by fire from the LORD on the spot. Moses' explanation: "I will be sanctified in them that come nigh me, and before all the people I will be glorified." Aaron holds his peace. The chapter closes with the wine-prohibition for priests on duty and the priestly responsibility to teach the difference between holy and unholy, clean and unclean — the catastrophe re-orienting the priesthood to its discernment-vocation.

### Chapter 11 — Clean and Unclean Animals

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, restoration

Israel's dietary purity laws. Land animals must part the hoof and chew the cud (so the camel, hare, coney, and swine are excluded); water creatures must have fins and scales; an extensive list of unclean birds; the creeping things prohibited. The chapter's theological grounding (11:44-45): "ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy." The food-rules embody at the table the holiness-distinction the priesthood is to teach.
